title: Carrying the head home
hook: Bhai Jaita carries the Guru's head to Anandpur, and Lakhi Shah burns his own house to cremate the body

segments.voice: Yesterday, Chandni Chowk, where the ninth Guru gave his head but not his faith. Your line was for another's faith.

After the Guru was killed in Chandni Chowk, his body lay in the square under guard. Tradition says the authorities meant it as a warning, and that nobody dared go near it. The Sikhs in Delhi were watched and afraid. When someone dies far from home, someone has to bring them back: the long road, the sitting with the body. It's one of the most loving and least noticed jobs there is. And that night, two men decided the Guru would not be left there.
screen: `THE BODY IN THE SQUARE.` → `SOMEONE HAS TO BRING THEM BACK.` → `TWO MEN, ONE NIGHT.`

segments.voice: The first was Bhai Jaita, a Sikh from a community that society treated as low caste. Tradition says that in the confusion of a dust storm that night, he slipped through, took up the Guru's head, wrapped it, and set off for Anandpur, hundreds of miles away, traveling in secret, mostly at night. There the young Gobind Rai, now the tenth Guru at nine years old, received his father's head. Tradition says he embraced Jaita and spoke a line Sikhs still repeat: Rangrete Guru ke bete. The Rangretas, Jaita's own community, are the Guru's own sons. A boy honoring a man the world looked down on, calling him family. Jaita later took initiation and became Bhai Jiwan Singh. The second man was Lakhi Shah, a wealthy trader who carried goods by bullock cart. In the same storm, tradition says, he and his sons hid the Guru's body in a cart under a load of cotton and drove it to their house outside the city. A public cremation would have brought soldiers. So Lakhi Shah built a pyre inside his own home, laid the Guru's body in it, and set his house on fire. To the neighbors, it looked like an accident. It was his home, given as a funeral. Gurdwara Rakab Ganj stands there today, near the Parliament of India. One man carried the head to a nine-year-old son. One burned down everything he had. Neither was a Guru, and both brought him home. With them, the story of the ninth Guru ends.
screen: `BHAI JAITA TAKES THE HEAD.` · `RANGRETE GURU KE BETE.` · `LAKHI SHAH'S CART OF COTTON.` · `A HOUSE GIVEN AS A FUNERAL.` · then, large: `BRING HIM HOME.`

segments.voice: Think of a loving task nobody wants to do and nobody will thank you for: visiting someone difficult, sorting a relative's things, sitting with someone in a hospital, calling the family nobody calls. Picture yourself doing it quietly, unseen, like a man walking through a dust storm, and let it feel possible.
Bhai Jaita. The Sikh who carried Guru Tegh Bahadur's head from Delhi to Anandpur, whom the young Guru called a son of the Guru.
Your line: bring him home. A head carried by night, and a house given as a funeral. Day eighty, done.

howItsDone: Sikhs honor Bhai Jaita and Lakhi Shah Vanjara at Gurdwara Sis Ganj in Anandpur Sahib, where the head was cremated, and Gurdwara Rakab Ganj in Delhi, where the body was.
